summary: An interactive 3D Earth LLM navigator using NASA FIRMS (VIIRS & MODIS) to monitor live global fires, harmonize cross-sensor FRP data with ML, and forecast 7-day wildfire risks.
details:
What does it do / how does it work? PyroCopilot is a web application that visualizes global fires and thermal anomalies on a 3D globe and presents 7-day fire risk forecasts. An AI also answers natural language questions.

  1. Data Acquisition: Uses near-real-time VIIRS (NOAA-20/21) detections and historical MODIS/VIIRS data from NASA FIRMS, along with NASA POWER for city-level weather data.
  2. Detection Model: Classifies whether a detection is a vegetation fire or a static heat source (such as a factory).
  3. Slash-and-Burn Identification: Distinguishes between slash-and-burn/repeated agricultural burning, wildfires, and industrial heat sources based on spatial recurrence patterns.
  4. MODIS and VIIRS Integration: Harmonizes the FRP (Fire Radiative Power) of the two sensors using an XGBoost Tweedie model.
  5. Risk Forecasting: Estimates the probability of a fire occurring within a 50 km radius over the next 7 days using weather data from roughly the past 30 days and recent fire activity.
  6. AI Copilot: Gemini returns structured responses with map controls. For example, asking "Show me the Amazon" zooms into that region and provides an explanation. It also supports Japanese place-name aliases.

Benefits

  • Separating fire types (wildfires, slash-and-burn, industrial heat sources) reduces false alarms and overestimation.
  • In addition to showing "where it is burning now," it reveals "where the risk is high over the next 7 days."
  • Users can perform analysis without specialized knowledge, simply by interacting with the globe and conversing in Japanese or English.
  • Serverless static hosting and a BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) approach keep operational costs low and make the system easy for anyone to reproduce.

Intended impact

  • Enables disaster management/firefighting agencies, researchers, journalists, and citizens to intuitively understand fire situations.
  • Distinguishing slash-and-burn from wildfires supports monitoring and policy discussions regarding deforestation and peatland fires (e.g., in Borneo and Sumatra).
  • Lowers the barrier to accessing NASA's open data.

Tools, languages, hardware, software

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS
  • Data: NASA FIRMS (VIIRS/MODIS), NASA POWER
  • ML / Data Processing: LightGBM (detection & risk), XGBoost Tweedie (FRP harmonization; CV log-MAE ~0.883, log correlation ~0.658), Polars, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, matplotlib
  • Training Environment: Kaggle (training/kaggle_fire)
  • Visualization: D3.js v7, TopoJSON, custom 3D globe engine (globe_engine.js)
  • AI: Google Gemini API
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages (static site)

How is it creative?

  • Combines a 3D globe UI with a conversational AI that directly manipulates the map.
  • Categorizes thermal anomalies into "slash-and-burn, wildfire, and industrial," differentiating it from simple hotspot displays.
  • Statistically harmonizes different sensors (MODIS/VIIRS) so they can be treated as a long-term time series.
  • Shares feature engineering code between training and inference to prevent discrepancies between production and training.

Factors the team considered

  • Data Quality: Inter-sensor bias, false positives from static heat sources, and the skewed distribution of FRP (addressed using Tweedie loss).
  • Scalability and Cost: Minimizes operational overhead through static hosting and lightweight JSON delivery.
  • Accessibility: Bilingual support (Japanese/English) and an intuitive UI usable without specialized expertise
